ex: Khublei! Kumno ka sngi jong me?
n: Khublei is hello, thanks and bye at once. Kumno? on its own is the casual Shillong 'hi'.

ex: Khublei! Phi la thiah bha?
n: No fixed time-of-day greeting; Khublei works all day. Khublei mynstep is heard but sounds translated.

ex: Khublei. Nga lah ban ïarap ïa phi?
n: No 'good afternoon': Khublei is used at any hour.

ex: Thiah suk! Khublei.
n: Literally 'sleep peacefully'; said at bedtime. When parting at night, Leit suk / Shong suk as usual.

ex: Khublei Sam, phi long kumno?
n: me long kumno? to a close male friend, pha long kumno? to a female one.

ex: Phi long kumno? — Nga khlaiñ, khublei. Bad phi?
n: khlaiñ is strong, healthy: the standard 'fine'.

ex: Phi long kumno? — Ym sniew, khublei.
n: sniew is bad; Ym sniew is 'not bad'. Nga biang (I'm alright) also works. Less certain this is a set phrase.

t: Nga kmen ban ïakynduh bad phi
ex: Khublei, nga dei ka Anna. Nga kmen ban ïakynduh bad phi.
n: kmen is glad, ïakynduh is meet. Polite but a bit bookish; many just smile and say Khublei.

ex: Nga kmen ban ïakynduh bad phi. — Nga ruh.
n: Nga ruh (me too) is the natural return; ruh follows the word it stresses.

t: Nga sngewkmen ban ïakynduh bad phi
ex: Khublei, nga dei u David Lee. Nga sngewkmen ban ïakynduh bad phi.
n: sngewkmen (feel glad) is the more formal form; use with titles Bah or Kong.

ex: Hei Tom, kumno? Me long kumno?
n: me to a male friend, pha to a female. Kumno alone is the casual greeting.

t: Nga kmen ban ïohi ïa phi
ex: Hei Maria! Nga kmen ban ïohi ïa pha.
n: ïohi is see; pha to a female friend, me to a male.

ex: Khublei, bad khublei shibun na ka bynta baroh.
n: The one leaving says Shong suk, the one staying says Leit suk; Khublei covers both.

ex: Bha, ngin sa ïakynduh!
n: sa marks 'later'; the shorter Sa ïakynduh! is common among friends.

ex: Khublei. Leit suk!
n: No 'have a nice day': Leit suk (go well) is what a shopkeeper says to a leaving customer.

ex: Khublei na ka bynta ka kophi.
n: na ka bynta (for) plus a noun gives the reason for the thanks.

ex: Khublei shibun, me bha eh ka mynsiem.
n: bha ka mynsiem (good of heart) is 'kind'; pha to a female friend.

t: Khublei, ym don eiei / Ym don eiei
ex: Khublei! — Ym don eiei.
n: Literally 'it is nothing'. The reply often repeats Khublei first.

ex: Khublei ba phi la ap. — Ym don eiei.
Phi kwah ka sha? — Hooid, khublei.
n: Accepting takes khublei, not sngewbha: sngewbha is for asking, not for yes.

ex: Phi kwah biang ka cake? — Em, khublei.
n: biang here is 'again, another'; Em, khublei is polite enough on its own.

ex: Map, kane ka rel kaba leit sha London?
n: Map (pardon) does the job of 'excuse me' for attention and for passing.

ex: Map ïa nga, ka long ka bakla jong nga.
n: Map ïa nga (forgive me) is the real apology; Nga sngewsih is 'I feel bad'.

ex: Map, nga la pynpait ïa ka cup jong phi. — Ym don eiei.
n: pynpait (make broken) for breaking is my best guess; confirm with a speaker.

t: Map ïa nga ba nga wan lait
ex: Map ïa nga ba nga wan lait, ka bas kam shym la wan.
n: wan lait is 'come late'; kam shym la is 'it did not' (past negative).

ex: Map, ngam sngewthuh. Phi lah ban ong biang?

t: Phi lah ban kren kham suki, sngewbha?
ex: Phi lah ban kren kham suki, sngewbha? Ka ktien Khasi jong nga kam bha eh.
n: kham suki is 'more slowly'; sngewbha at the end softens.

t: Phi lah ban ong biang, sngewbha?
ex: Map, phi lah ban ong biang ïa kata, sngewbha?
n: ong biang is 'say again'.

t: Phi lah ban ong ïa ki dak, sngewbha?
ex: Ka kyrteng jait jong phi? Phi lah ban ong ïa ki dak, sngewbha?
n: No everyday 'spell' verb: ask to say the letters (dak), or thoh (write) it. kyrteng jait is the clan surname.

t: Ngam nang kren bun ka ktien English
ex: Map, ngam nang kren bun ka ktien English.
n: nang is 'know how to'; ka ktien is 'the language'.

ex: Khublei, nga dei u Tom. Aiu ka kyrteng jong phi?
n: Kaei ka kyrteng jong phi? is equally common.

ex: Phi wan nangno? Ka rukom kren jong phi ka itynnad.
n: nangno is 'from where'. rukom kren (way of speaking) is accent. Less certain of nangno vs na shano.

t: Katno snem pha? / Katno ka rta jong pha?
ex: Emma, katno snem pha?
n: Literally 'how many years you'; rta is age. pha to a girl, me to a boy, phi to an adult.

ex: Phi shong hangno? Hajan hangne?
n: shong is live, stay; hajan is near.

t: Phi trei aiu? / Aiu ka kam jong phi?
ex: Phi trei aiu? Phi dei u nongpule?
n: nongpule is student; ka nongpule for a woman.

ex: Phi don ki para shynrang ne ki para kynthei?
n: para alone is sibling; shynrang (male) and kynthei (female) narrow it.

ex: Naduh lano phi shong hangne?
n: Khasi asks 'since when', not 'how long'; no perfect needed.

ex: Nga wan na Italy. Bad phi?
Map, katno baje mynta?
n: baje is o'clock; the answer is Ka long lai baje (it's three).

ex: Kane ka bag ka itynnad. Katno ka dor?
n: dor is price.

t: Nga lah ban ïarap ïa phi?
ex: Khublei, nga lah ban ïarap ïa phi?
Phi kwah kiwei pat? — Em, ka la biang, khublei.
n: biang here is 'enough'; kiwei pat is 'anything else'.

t: Nga lah ban peit ïa ka menu, sngewbha?
ex: Khublei, nga lah ban peit ïa ka menu, sngewbha?
n: menu is said as in English.

t: Aiu ka bha ban bam hangne?
ex: Kane ka sien ba nyngkong ba nga wan hangne. Aiu ka bha ban bam?
n: No 'recommend' verb in daily speech: ask 'what is good to eat here'.

ex: Ngam bam doh. Don doh ha kane ka soup?
n: No common word for vegetarian; say 'I don't eat meat' (doh).

ex: Em shuh, khublei. Nga la dap.
n: dap is full; shuh after em is 'no more'.

t: Hangno ka bathroom? / Hangno ka toilet?
ex: Map, hangno ka bathroom?
n: Shillong speakers use the English words.

ex: Leit beit, bad ka bank ka don sha kti diang.
n: kti diang is left, kti mon is right.

ex: Nga kwah ban leit sha ka zoo. Hangno nga dei ban hiar?
n: hiar is 'get down', used for leaving a bus or taxi.

t: Aiu ka password jong ka wifi?
ex: Map, aiu ka password jong ka wifi?
Ïarap! Ïarap ïa nga, sngewbha!
n: Shouted ïarap (help) is my best rendering; people may also just yell Ko Blei!

t: Phi lah ban ïarap ïa nga?
ex: Map, phi lah ban ïarap ïa nga? Ngam tip shuh ïa ka lynti.
n: Ngam tip shuh ïa ka lynti is 'I don't know the way any more', the plain way to say lost.

ex: Nga donkam ïa u doktor. U khun jong nga u pang shibun.
n: pang is sick; u khun (masc.) for a son.

ex: Ka pang hangne, ha ka kpoh.
n: kpoh is belly, stomach; ka is the dummy subject for the pain.

ex: Ngam sngew khlaiñ. Ngan leit sha ïing.
n: Don't say Ngam sngew bha: sngewbha is 'please'. khlaiñ (well) avoids the clash.

ex: Khot ïa ka ambulance! Um ring mynsiem!
n: khot is call; ring mynsiem (draw breath) for breathing is my best guess.

ex: Map, nga la jah lynti. Hangno ka steshon?
n: jah lynti (lose the way) is my best rendering; Ngam tip ïa ka lynti is safer.

ex: Khmih! Ka kali!
n: khmih is look, sumar is take care; less certain which is shouted more.

ex: Phi paw sngewsih. Aiu ka jia?
n: jia is happen: 'what happened?'. paw is look, seem.

ex: Phi khlaiñ? Phi paw kumba phi pang.
n: Literally 'are you well'; rises at the end.

ex: Kmen ka sngi kha! Kane ka jingai na ka bynta jong phi.
n: sngi kha is birthday; many say Happy birthday in English. jingai is gift.

ex: Phi la pass ka test? Bha eh!
n: pass (an exam) is used as in English.

ex: Shim ka syrbaïn. Ka dang slap.
n: ka is the dummy subject; dang makes it 'is raining now'.

t: Ka suiñbneng ka bha mynta, ne em?
ex: Ka suiñbneng ka bha mynta, ne em?
n: ne em (or not) is the Khasi tag question.

t: Aiu ka nombor phone jong phi?
ex: Aiu ka nombor phone jong phi? Ngan phah message ïa phi.
n: phah is send.

ex: Map, ngam sngew ïa phi. Don bun ka jingsawa hangne.
n: sngew is both hear and feel; jingsawa is noise, sound.

t: Map, ngam shym la shim ïa ka phone jong phi
ex: Map, ngam shym la shim ïa ka phone jong phi. Aiu ka jia?
n: No 'miss a call' verb: say 'I didn't take your phone (call)'.

t: Nga lah ban kylli ïa phi kawei?
ex: Map, nga lah ban kylli ïa phi kawei?
n: kylli is ask; kawei (one) stands for 'a question'.

ex: Bha, bam janmiet ha ka sngi Friday. Katno baje ngin ïakynduh?

t: Ka phone jong nga ka jan lut ka charge
ex: Nga hap ban leit, ka phone jong nga ka jan lut ka charge.
n: jan is 'almost'; lut is 'run out'. charge is the English word.

ex: Hmm, ap khyndiat, nga pyrkhat... ka long ha ka sngi Tuesday.
Ap khyndiat, ngan sa shim ka pen.
Ap shi minit, nga dang wan!
n: nga dang wan (I'm coming) uses dang for the in-progress sense.

ex: Ap khyndiat, ngan peit.
n: Same phrase on the phone; ap is wait.

ex: Map? Ngam shym la sngew.
n: Map with a rising tone is the polite 'pardon?'.

ex: Aiu? Phi lah ban ong biang?
n: Bare Aiu? (what?) is fine with friends, blunt with elders.

ex: Aiu kata? Ngam tip ïa kata ka ktien.
n: ktien is both word and language.

ex: Bha, to ngi leit.
n: Bha (good) is the everyday 'okay'.

ex: Nga lah ban shong hangne? — Hooid hi, shong noh.
n: hi adds emphasis; less certain this is the most common 'of course'.

ex: Phi lah ban ai ïa ka mluh? — Hooid.
n: mluh is salt.

ex: Nga ieid ïa kane ka jingrwai. — Nga ruh!
Ngam ieid ïa ka kophi. — Nga ruh em.
n: Literally 'me also not'; Nga ruh ngam ieid (I don't like it either) is the fuller form.

ex: Bha, kumta ka bas kan leit ha khyndai baje.
n: kumta (so) often follows to sum up what was agreed.

ex: Map, ngam tip.
Phin wan mynta ka miet? — Lehse.
Ka plie ha ka sngi Sunday? — Ngam tip shisha.

t: Kata ka jingpyrkhat kaba bha / Bha
ex: To ngi shim ka taxi. — Bha, kata ka jingpyrkhat kaba bha.
n: Plain Bha! is the everyday short form.

ex: Phi la ïoh ka kam? Kata ka bha shibun!
Ko Blei! Nga la klet ïa ki chabi.
n: Ko Blei (O God) is the common alarm cry; klet is forget.

ex: Te... ngam tip shisha.
n: te (then, so) is the stalling word.

ex: Ha ka jingshisha, nga wan na Canada, ym na US.
Pizza ha hynñiew baje? — Bha!
Ngan ïohi ïa me hangta. — Cool.
n: Young Shillong speakers use English cool; Bha is the plain Khasi.

ex: Wow! Ka ïing jong me ka itynnad shibun.
n: itynnad is beautiful; English wow is common in speech.

ex: Ngan wan ha phra baje. Ka bha?
Nga la khie, bad hadien kata nga la bam ka jingbam mynstep.
n: khie is get up; jingbam mynstep is breakfast.

ex: Nga ieid ïa ka sha, hynrei ngam ieid ïa ka kophi.
Nga thait namar ba nga la trei slem.
n: thait is tired; slem is long, late.

ex: Nga kren ka ktien French. Nga kren khyndiat ka ktien German ruh.
n: ruh follows the word it stresses: Nga ruh would mean 'I too'.

ex: Nyngkong nga sum, hadien kata nga kup jain.
n: sum is bathe; kup jain for getting dressed is my best guess.
